sections.html:
Speed in Waukesha mostly depends on who is buying. Someone paying cash needs no mortgage underwriting and no lender's appraisal, so that deal tends to finish first. A listing or an owner sale brings showings, an inspection and a buyer's mortgage into the timeline. No matter the route, the house carries three Wisconsin documents to the finish line: a condition report, an electronic transfer return and a recorded deed. Learn them now and you can judge each offer by the money you actually walk away with.

Waukesha is the county seat of Waukesha County, in the Milwaukee metropolitan area. The 2025 population estimate is 70,872, a little under the 71,158 counted in 2020. Water comes up with buyers: the city switched from groundwater to Lake Michigan supply in 2023, and typical bills were projected to climb about 50 percent between 2023 and 2027, so be ready for utility cost questions.

Waukesha's median owner-occupied home was valued at $315,500 over 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 58.8 percent of the housing units. There are 30,567 households, median gross rent is $1,219 and median household income is $83,837 in 2024 dollars. Those are citywide numbers. Condition, lot size and street can push your house far above or below them, so use the median as a loose yardstick and get written offers before you decide anything.

sections.h2: What Wisconsin requires when you sell in Waukesha
sections.html:
If the building has four units or fewer, the seller owes the buyer a completed real estate condition report. Wis. Stat. chapter 709 allows 10 days from the date the contract is accepted. When it fails to show up, the buyer gets two business days after that stretch to cancel and take deposits back.

A seller acting as personal representative, trustee, conservator or court-supervised fiduciary, who never lived there, can skip the form. So can parties to any transfer that the fee statute exempts. If you inherited a house here and never lived in it, your probate attorney or title company can say whether that exception covers you.

The state also bills the grantor a real estate transfer fee. Section 77.22 fixes the rate at 30 cents per $100 of value, or $3 per $1,000, and the register of deeds takes the money when it records. Grantor and grantee each sign the electronic return. Section 77.24 divides the proceeds: 20 percent for the county, the remainder for the state.

The city clerk and treasurer send the bills and collect payments from mid-December until July 31. After that date the records pass to the Waukesha County Treasurer. Mailing happens by mid-December. Pay in full or make the first installment by January 31, then follow with installments on March 31 and May 31. The dates on your own bill are posted on the city's tax page.

The city keeps only part of what you pay. This table shows how the levy is divided:

Taxing bodyRate per $1,000Share of tax dollar
City of Waukesha$7.7953.8%
Waukesha School District$5.1235.41%
Waukesha County$1.308.99%
Waukesha County Technical College$0.251.75%

Together the rates total $14.46 per $1,000. A state credit of $1.04 brings the net rate to $13.42. You can pay on the county tax website, inside a Waukesha State Bank branch, by mail, in either 24-hour drop box (City Hall or the library), or in person at 201 Delafield Street. Your title company calculates how the current year's bill is split.

sections.h2: Selling a Waukesha house with taxes unpaid
sections.html:
An unpaid tax bill will not block a sale, though it reshuffles the steps. Once July 31 passes, unpaid bills move from the city to the Waukesha County Treasurer, so that is where a payoff figure comes from. Get that number before you sign a contract. The title company can then deduct it from what you receive, and the buyer gets a house with nothing owed.

Cash buyers see this situation often and can work around it, because they do not wait on a lender's underwriting. Still, put the unpaid balance in writing in the offer so both sides agree on who clears it. A seller who knows the real payoff can then compare a quick cash price to a slower listing without guessing at what the final check will be.

Each property gets its value from the assessor, who neither sets nor collects the tax. State law asks for the full value a property would ordinarily bring in a private sale. Ask the assessor's office for this year's open book and Board of Review dates.

Think the number is off before you sell? The city takes an online Request for Property Review for the January 1, 2027 assessment date. Property record cards on the assessor's site show lot size, building details and tax history, and they make a useful attachment when you weigh offers.

sections.h2: City rules that can slow a Waukesha sale
sections.html:
Permits and property maintenance matter most. The city wants inspections on new construction, alterations and repairs, on electrical, plumbing and HVAC jobs, and on a change in occupancy. A buyer's inspector may ask about unpermitted work, so assemble your permit history early.

The city's maintenance rules sit in Chapter 17 of its code. It makes the owner responsible for keeping the structure and exterior in the condition the chapter describes, and it bars occupancy of unsafe or unsanitary premises. Inspectors take calls on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the city site carries forms to report tall grass and other complaints. Closing out open violations before you list takes away one excuse for a lower offer.

  • Building permits and occupancy for one- and two-family homes: 262-524-3530.
  • Electrical permits: 262-524-3533. Plumbing permits: 262-524-3534.
  • Property maintenance inspectors: 262-524-3528, 262-524-3532 and 262-524-3545.

sections.h2: How recording a deed works in Waukesha County
sections.html:
Recording happens at the Waukesha County Register of Deeds. A standard document is $30, payable by check or money order and nothing else. Add any transfer fee from your return receipt to that same payment. Reach the office at 262-548-7585 or recording@waukeshacounty.gov. It serves the public from 8:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m. on weekdays.

Do not expect blank deeds or legal advice at the counter. A title company or a real estate attorney usually prepares the deed and files the return. E-recording returns the document right away. Paper originals take two to three weeks to return, as long as a stamped return envelope is enclosed.

sections.h2: What to have ready before you list
sections.html:
Waukesha buyers keep asking for the same few papers. Pull your permit history, the receipts for any big repair, and a recent tax bill. Print the record card from the assessor's site, since it lists the lot size and building details. If you took out work without a permit, learn what the inspection office needs before a buyer's inspector brings it up.

Expect questions about water bills. If anything on the property sits under an open city notice, clear it first, since a clean file keeps a nervous buyer from asking for a credit. If the house came through an estate, add the probate papers to the folder now so the closing date does not slip.

When two or three bids land in the same week, a plain worksheet beats a gut feeling. For each bid, record the price, closing date, lender involvement, expected repairs, and who pays for title and recording. A higher number from a financed buyer can still lose to a lower cash number if the cash deal closes sooner and costs you less in mortgage payments, taxes and upkeep while you wait.

Ask each buyer how they handle the condition report. A buyer who knows the ten-day rule and the two-business-day cancel right will not be surprised by it. Ask also whether they plan to use their own title company or yours, since that choice decides who files the electronic return and who delivers the deed to the register for recording. Get every answer in writing, and save the bids you turn down in case the first deal collapses.

sections.h2: From signed contract to closing day
sections.html: Acceptance of an offer starts the report clock, so complete that form first. Next, line up your permit history, the newest tax bill and mortgage payoff details. While the title company runs its search, settle the tax split with the buyer. Closing day brings your signature on the deed, an online return, and a recording at the register of deeds. If the house is a cash sale, those same steps happen with no appraisal or underwriting to hold up the date.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell a house in Waukesha?
faqs.a: The buyer sets the pace. Without a lender there is no loan approval or appraisal, but a financed listing waits on showings, inspections and underwriting. Under both, expect the report deadline of 10 days from acceptance.

faqs.q: Do I have to fill out a condition report in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: In most sales, yes. The duty covers owners of residential property with one to four units. Personal representatives and trustees who never lived there are excused, and so are transfers that the fee statute exempts.

faqs.q: How much is the Wisconsin transfer fee on a Waukesha sale?
faqs.a: The seller's side of a Waukesha deal includes a 30-cent charge on every $100 of value, paid when the deed is recorded. Some gifts and inheritances, such as a transfer by will, are exempt under s. 77.25.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property taxes to in Waukesha?
faqs.a: The City of Waukesha Clerk/Treasurer takes payments from mid-December through July 31. After that the Waukesha County Treasurer takes over delinquent real estate taxes. Options include online, mail, a Waukesha State Bank branch, a drop box or the City Hall window.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed after I sell in Waukesha?
faqs.a: The county's Register of Deeds handles it. Plan on $30 for the deed, paid by check or money order, with any transfer fee included and the return receipt attached. Most sellers let the title company handle that step.
